description: Grupo de compañeros interesados en aprender y desarrollar juntos.
summary: XionMetrical is a visual health-monitoring tool for astronauts on a Mars mission, where a message to Earth can take up to 20 minutes each way. It gathers 10 health indicators that cover NASA’s five hazards of human spaceflight, compares every value with the astronaut’s own baseline (built during the first 30 days) and flags drift early with a traffic light that always uses a shape and a word, never color alone. Each state comes with short guidance in four layers — why it matters, what to do now, when to escalate and how to measure — and every line shows its source (NASA, health agencies, or the team’s own rule, marked “XionMetrical rule”). It answers the challenge by helping crews assess their own health and act on board first, without waiting for Earth. The website includes an interactive demo with 1,080 days of simulated data (180 days out, 720 on the surface, 180 back). Prototype; not a medical device.
details:
What it does. XionMetrical helps an astronaut answer one question every day: is my body drifting away from my own normal? On a Mars mission the crew cannot count on real-time help from Earth, so the tool gives an early warning against each astronaut’s personal baseline, explains why it matters and says what to do, with a source for every line.

Interface. A clickable 2D body map (heart, brain, lungs, blood, muscles, whole body and more) shows each area’s traffic-light state for the selected mission day, and its areas can be opened from the keyboard. For each indicator, a panel shows the day’s value, your baseline band, the cited reference and a trend chart.

How it works.

Personal baseline. Days 1–30 build a band for each indicator: mean ± 1.5 standard deviations (with a small minimum width at the measurement’s resolution).

Traffic light (shape + word). Normal (green circle ✓) — inside your band and inside published limits. Drifting (yellow triangle !) — outside your band 2+ days in a row, within 10% of a published limit, or a 14-day trend that would cross the limit within 30 days. Act now (red octagon !) — beyond a published limit (NASA or general health). A value can be inside the general adult range and still be yellow because it moved away from your baseline: that is the core idea.

Sourced guidance in 4 layers: status and why, what to do now, when to escalate, how to measure. Texts are fixed and written from the cited sources; they are never generated inside the app. Where no countermeasure is published, the app says so and refers to the Crew Medical Officer. No diagnosis, no medication, no doses.

Emergency guide (chest pain or collapse): 8 steps — act on board first, then send a store-and-forward message to the flight surgeon on Earth without waiting for the reply.

Daily check-in: measurement reminders (on waking, before sleep, weekly; radiation and CO₂ come from sensors) and a “Log today’s measurements” form (heart rate, sleep, mood) checked instantly with the same rule. Nothing typed is stored or sent.

The 10 indicators and NASA’s 5 hazards. Resting heart rate, blood pressure, body temperature, sleep, mood (self-rated 1–5), fasting glucose, cumulative radiation dose, CO₂ near you, strength and fitness, and food intake and body mass — together they cover space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity fields, and hostile and closed environments.

Demo scenario (simulated data). One example astronaut, 1,080 days. On days 113–118 resting heart rate, blood pressure, sleep and mood drift; on day 115 the app shows “Resting heart rate above your baseline · 3 days” while the heart rate is still inside the 60–100 bpm range for adults on Earth. Later in the mission the cumulative radiation dose reaches NASA’s 600 mSv career limit on day 671, during the surface stay (≈ 1.5 mSv/day in transit and ≈ 0.67 mSv/day on the surface, from NASA figures). Automated tests check this scenario and that no other alerts appear in the 1,080 days beyond the designed CO₂ pockets and dose limits.

Benefits. Earlier and personal warnings instead of fixed population ranges; crew autonomy despite the communication delay; every tip traceable to a source; accessible design (shape and word for each state, keyboard-operable body map, responsive layout).

Goals and next steps. Feed the same baseline engine with wearable sensors instead of typing, like the wearable technology NASA already tests on the space station; and send a delayed (store-and-forward) summary to flight surgeons on Earth, so the crew acts on board first and the ground team follows up.

Tools, languages, hardware and software. TypeScript; React 19 and Next.js 16 (static export); Tailwind CSS 4; Node.js 24 test runner; hand-written SVG for the charts and the body map (no chart libraries, no external images or fonts); GitHub and GitHub Pages. Video: vector animation rendered frame by frame with Playwright and Chrome, narration with Piper TTS (voice en_US-joe-medium), sound effects synthesized by code, and FFmpeg. AI tools: Claude Code (Anthropic) and, in an early background chat, Gemini (Google); details in Use of SI. Hardware: a standard Windows 11 computer; no special hardware.
